The core theorem of the paper is that under average-score evaluation with a proper scoring rule, the optimal predictor is deterministic and equal to the conditional probability q_x. This follows from Wald’s decision theory and Duda & Hart’s ERM framework. The derivation begins with the average score decomposition S_avg = Σ_{x∈X} (n_x/N){q_x S(p(x),1) + (1-q_x)S(p(x),0)}, where each term is minimized by setting p*(x) = q_x. For Brier scoring, S(p,y) = (p-y)^2, so the minimizer is indeed q_x. This establishes that the statistical predictor is optimal by definition under these conditions. The failure mode arises when the assumptions are violated—such as non-stationarity, improper scoring rules, or insufficient data. In such cases, the deterministic mapping breaks down, leading to suboptimal predictions. The paper further notes that expert judgment often fails because it lacks the same data access and evaluation criteria, and introduces concepts like staleness and override auditing to maintain performance.
